issues.legal_issue: The State may not allot public land as largesse through a selective process that excludes similarly eligible organisations from competing.
material_facts: An organisation sought reservation of public land for a proposed training institute, and the Government reserved and allotted land to it without advertising for applications or inviting similarly situated organisations to participate.
The notices published invited objections to the proposed reservation or allotment, but did not invite competing applications.
The allotment process and a substantial waiver of the premium were undertaken in circumstances the Court found showed political favouritism.
issues.conclusion: The allotment violated Article 14 because it was made without a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory process, and the Court declared it illegal and quashed it.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 requires the State to distribute public largesse, including land, under a sound, transparent and discernible policy applied by a non-discriminatory method. The State cannot entertain an individual application while excluding other eligible claimants; as a matter of course, it must publicise eligibility and allow similarly situated claimants to participate, whether allotment is by auction or otherwise. The Court relied on R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) 3 SCC 489; Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India (1979) 3 SCC 489; Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of J&K (1980) 4 SCC 1; Common Cause v. Union of India (1996) 6 SCC 530; Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P. (1991) 1 SCC 212; L.I.C. of India v. Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995) 5 SCC 482; and New India Public School v. HUDA (1996) 5 SCC 510. It also referred to the constitutional commitments to equality and the distribution of community resources for the common good under Article 39(b).

predicates.public_land_allotment_challenge: A proceeding challenges a public authority's allotment of public land.
predicates.individual_application_led_to_selective_: A person or organisation applied for land and the authority proceeded to allot it to that applicant.
predicates.no_open_invitation_to_similarly_eligible: The authority did not publicly invite similarly eligible claimants to compete for the allotment.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a public land allotment made on an individual application without an open invitation to similarly eligible claimants, the allotment is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A development plan cannot be modified under the public-project ground to facilitate a private institution's project that is outside the specified public-project categories.
material_facts: The development plan designated the land for public and semi-public health use.
The land had been allotted to a private trust for its institute before the Government modified the plan to enable that use.
The modification was made under the provision concerning government projects, state-development projects and schemes of the development authority, but the institute was not such a project or scheme.
issues.conclusion: The modification was ultra vires the statutory power invoked, and the Court quashed the relevant notifications.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 14 and 17 establish the preparation and land-use framework for development plans, and Section 25(1) requires land use to conform to the operative plan. Section 23-A(1)(a) permits modification for specified government or state-development projects and development-authority schemes; it is not a general power to alter a plan for a private project. Section 23-A(1)(b) separately permits a modification on an application where the proposed activity or scheme is considered beneficial to society by the Government or Director on the advice of the designated committee. Section 23-A(2) prescribes public notice, consideration of objections and suggestions, and a hearing for affected persons. The Court relied on these statutory provisions and the planning framework; it cited no earlier case for this issue.

predicates.development_plan_modification_challenge: A proceeding challenges a modification of an operative development plan.
predicates.plan_changed_to_enable_a_private_institu: The authority changed the plan to permit a private institution's project on land previously designated for another use.
predicates.project_is_not_a_government_project_stat: The project enabled by the change is not a government project, a state-development project, or a development-authority scheme.

issues.definition: A challenged plan modification made to enable a private institution's project outside the specified public-project categories is ultra vires.

issues.legal_issue: A public-interest petitioner has standing to seek review of an exercise of official power that raises a question of public importance.
material_facts: The petitioner was a public-spirited organisation that engaged in public welfare activities.
It challenged the allotment of public land and had also challenged another similar allotment.
The challenge raised issues concerning the exercise of power by State officials.
issues.conclusion: The challenge to the petitioner's standing was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: A person may raise a question of public importance involving the exercise of power by public officials even if the person also has a private interest in the matter. The Court relied on Shivajirao Nilangekar Patil v. Mahesh Madhav Gosavi (1987) 1 SCC 227.

predicates.public_law_petition_challenging_official: A proceeding asks a court to review the exercise of power by public officials.
predicates.petitioner_is_public_spirited: The petitioner engages in public-interest or public-welfare activity.
predicates.issue_involves_public_importance: The challenge raises a matter of public importance concerning official power.

issues.definition: A petitioner has standing to bring a public-law challenge to official power if the petitioner is public-spirited or the issue involves public importance.

issues.legal_issue: Prospective-only relief cannot preserve a public land allotment found to result from a gross violation of equality and political favouritism.
material_facts: The land allotment was made without an open process for similarly eligible organisations to compete.
The Court found that the process involved a gross violation of Article 14 and favouritism and nepotism.

The respondent sought to have the ruling applied only prospectively, relying on an earlier decision involving allotments made against a different background, including allottees who had altered their position.
issues.conclusion: The Court refused to apply prospective overruling to preserve the allotment and quashed it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Harsh Dhingra v. State of Haryana (2001) 9 SCC 550, where the allotments were made against the background of an earlier High Court judgment and allottees had altered their position. It held that prospective-only treatment was not appropriate for an allotment found to be the product of a gross violation of Article 14 and favouritism.

predicates.public_land_allotment_challenge: A proceeding challenges a public authority's allotment of public land.
predicates.allotment_involves_gross_equality_violat: The allotment process excluded fair competition and the authority's conduct amounted to a gross equality violation involving favouritism.

issues.definition: When a challenged public land allotment involves a gross equality violation and favouritism, prospective-only relief is unavailable to preserve it.
